string-array.name: policy_privacy
string-array.item: Yew runs on your own computer, and Yew on your phone (iPhone or Android) connects only to Yew on your own computer. Tenon AI does not collect or receive your content in Yew, and Yew contains no analytics, telemetry or reporting code.

Data kept on your computer: sessions, messages, tool call records, permissions you granted, letters between sessions, the decisions you make in the approval center, scheduled tasks and settings are stored in a database in Yew\'s data folder (~/.yew by default); provider API keys, and the access tokens, refresh tokens and client registrations Yew gets when you sign in to an MCP server in your browser, are stored in the system keychain; MCP server settings are kept in mcp.json in the data folder, including keys you enter and the ID and secret of a Google client you created yourself; very long command output is stored in the tmp folder of the data folder; every version of the artifacts sessions save (documents, pages, data and charts) is stored in its artifacts folder. The profile of Yew\'s built-in browser (cookies, cache and history of the sites you signed in to there) is stored in the browser folder of the data folder. When you set Yew to start at login with yew service, its service log (start-up, errors and relay connection lines, without conversation content) is stored in the logs folder of the data folder. This data stays until you delete it. If you set a decision log file in Settings, Yew adds each decision to that file.

Phone access: when you turn on phone access on your computer, Yew on the computer connects to a relay, and Yew on your phone talks to it through the relay. The default relay is run by Tenon AI; you can also run your own. The two ends are encrypted end to end: the relay only passes ciphertext along and can neither read nor keep the content. For network security, the relay run by Tenon AI keeps a connection log: the time, the IP address, the path requested (which carries your computer\'s identifier, a hash of its public key) and the status, without content, deleted automatically after 184 days. The relay server is in mainland China. Yew on the computer records each paired phone: its name, public key, when it was paired and when it last connected. Yew on iPhone keeps the pairing and its own key in the iOS keychain, on that device only. With notifications on, Yew on iPhone gives the push token it got from Apple to your computer over the encrypted channel, and the computer keeps it; the computer encrypts what a notification says for that iPhone and hands it to Apple\'s push service through the relay. The relay and Apple handle the push token and the ciphertext, and cannot read what the notification says. Yew on Android keeps the pairing and its own key in a private file of the app, encrypted with a key in the Android Keystore, on that device only; it is left out of system backups and device transfers. Yew on Android uses no push service and has no push token: with notifications on, a foreground service keeps a connection to the relay open in the background, and the computer sends what a notification says to the phone over the end-to-end encrypted channel; the relay only passes ciphertext along. Android shows a standing notification for this connection, and notifications do not arrive while the system has stopped Yew. Scanning the pairing QR code uses the camera; the picture is read on the phone and is neither kept nor sent. The phone also remembers whether notifications are on and the ids of the items it has already seen, without their content.

Data sent to third parties: the model provider you choose for a session receives the conversation sent to it, including files the session read, command output, what MCP tools return (such as the emails, events and files in a mailbox, calendar or drive you connected), and the page content and screenshots a session obtains when it uses the browser and computer control tools; a screenshot captures whatever is on the screen at that moment, including other apps\' windows; that provider\'s privacy policy applies. The default provider, DeepSeek, is a service of the Chinese company DeepSeek; how it handles and stores this content is set out in its privacy policy. If you choose a provider outside mainland China, this content goes abroad. When a session fetches a web page or opens one in the built-in browser, that site receives the request; a site you signed in to in the built-in browser receives requests that carry your sign-in. Once you save a key for a search service, that service receives the query when a session searches the web, and its privacy policy applies; with a search service outside mainland China (Tavily, Brave), the query goes abroad. By default Yew starts two open-source MCP servers: a browser (Microsoft\'s Playwright MCP) and computer control (computer-use-mcp). They run on your computer, and you can turn them off in Settings. Yew downloads and installs these two, and the common servers you add with one click that run on your computer, from npm the first time it uses them; npm receives the download request. An MCP server you add (it is written in mcp.json) receives what a session passes to its tools, and a service you signed in to in your browser receives requests made with your account. These services\' own privacy policies apply; with a service outside mainland China (such as Google, Linear or Vercel), what is passed to it goes abroad. These tools ask you before each call, until you choose Always allow for a tool; the clicks, typing and key presses of computer control, and MCP tools that Yew recognizes as sending, publishing or deleting something, cannot be set to Always allow and ask every time.

Access, export and deletion: you can look at the files in the data folder directly. To delete a provider\'s key, delete it in Settings or run yew key delete; to remove a paired phone, remove it under Phone access on the computer, or unpair on the phone; to sign out of an MCP server, choose Sign out under MCP servers: where the service supports it, Yew first asks it to cancel the tokens, then deletes the ones kept on this computer; to make sure the access you granted is revoked, check or remove it in that service\'s account settings; to clear the built-in browser\'s sign-ins, delete the browser folder in the data folder; to delete everything, stop yew serve and delete the data folder. If you upgraded from Jig, also delete ~/.jig (usually just a link to the new folder; if Jig was running during the upgrade, the data may still be there) and the entries in the system keychain whose service name is asia.tenon.jig.

string-array.name: policy_terms
string-array.item: Yew is open source under the MIT License; see the LICENSE file in the code repository. Under that license you may use, copy, modify and distribute Yew. Yew is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, and to the extent the law allows we are not liable for losses arising from its use.

Yew reads and writes files, runs commands and goes online as you allow. Choose a suitable workspace and permission rules for each session; deleting files, pushing, publishing and similar operations always ask you first. The browser and computer control tools, and MCP servers you signed in to, can act with your sign-ins in web pages, other apps and those services, including sending, submitting, buying and deleting; think before you choose Always allow for them, and keep an eye on what the session is doing. The model provider you choose and the MCP servers you connect apply their own terms.

Tenon AI provides the default relay free of charge, only for Yew\'s phone access. It is provided as is, and we may change or stop it; connections that abuse it may be limited or closed. You can also run your own relay.
The Yew and Tenon AI names and logos are not licensed under the MIT License.
